## Diagnostic guidance (2025-05) · Reading BI-RADS assessment categories and the action each requires

Scope: how to interpret the final assessment category on a breast imaging report and
what management follows from it. This document concerns report interpretation only; it
does not tell you which imaging test to order first for a given symptom.

1. Category 0 — incomplete. The study cannot be finalized without additional views,
   ultrasound, or comparison with prior examinations. Category 0 is a workflow state,
   not a statement of risk. It is expected in screening recall and should be uncommon
   as the final result of a diagnostic study.
2. Category 1 — negative. Nothing to report. Return to the patient's routine screening
   interval.
3. Category 2 — benign. A specific benign entity is named: a coarsely calcified
   involuting fibroadenoma, a simple cyst, an intramammary lymph node, an oil cyst of
   fat necrosis, or a stable postsurgical scar. Management is identical to category 1 —
   routine screening — and no follow-up imaging is generated by the finding itself.
4. Category 3 — probably benign, carrying under roughly 2% likelihood of malignancy.
   The action is short-interval surveillance, conventionally at 6 months, then 12 and
   24 months, before the finding is downgraded to benign. Category 3 may be assigned
   only after a complete diagnostic workup, never off a screening study alone, and is
   inappropriate for a mass the patient can feel.
5. Category 4 — suspicious. Likelihood of malignancy spans roughly 2% to 95%, and
   tissue diagnosis is required. The subdivisions matter for counselling and for
   judging concordance afterwards: 4A low suspicion, 4B moderate suspicion, 4C high
   suspicion but short of classic malignant morphology.
6. Category 5 — highly suggestive of malignancy, at or above 95%. Biopsy is required,
   and surgical planning may proceed in parallel. A benign pathology result from a
   category 5 lesion is discordant by definition and mandates excision.
7. Category 6 — known biopsy-proven malignancy. It is applied to imaging performed
   after diagnosis, such as extent-of-disease mapping or response assessment during
   neoadjuvant therapy. It never means "biopsy again."
8. When a study shows several findings, the overall assessment takes the most abnormal
   category, and each breast is assessed separately.
9. Categories 4 and 5 require documented, tracked communication to the referring
   clinician; an unactioned suspicious report is a system failure, not a patient one.

## Case record 2025-04-08 · 71F · screen-detected 9 mm luminal A carcinoma, radiotherapy omission

**Presentation.** A 71-year-old postmenopausal woman attended routine screening mammography
with no breast symptoms. She had never taken menopausal hormone therapy, had two children
with first birth at 26, and reported no family history of breast or ovarian cancer.
Comorbidities were well-controlled hypertension and osteopenia under surveillance.

**Workup.** Screening mammography showed a new 9 mm irregular mass with indistinct margins
in the lower inner quadrant of the left breast, absent on the prior study two years earlier;
background density was scattered fibroglandular. Diagnostic magnification and spot-compression
views confirmed a persistent mass with no associated calcifications. Targeted ultrasound
demonstrated a 9 mm hypoechoic mass, taller-than-wide but without posterior shadowing,
assessed BI-RADS 4A. Axillary ultrasound was normal, with all visualised nodes showing
preserved fatty hila. Ultrasound-guided core biopsy with clip placement was performed. No MRI
was obtained; the lesion was well characterised and the breast was not dense.

**Pathology.** Invasive ductal carcinoma, grade 1, with prominent tubule formation. ER 95%,
PR 80%, HER2 IHC 1+ (negative), Ki-67 8%. No lymphovascular invasion.

**Course.** Wire-localised breast-conserving surgery with sentinel lymph node biopsy. Final
pathology: 8 mm invasive carcinoma, all margins clear, 0/2 sentinel nodes negative — pT1b
pN0. A 21-gene recurrence score assay returned a low result, so adjuvant chemotherapy was not
offered. The multidisciplinary discussion then centred on radiotherapy. With age above 70, a
tumour under 2 cm, node-negative and strongly ER-positive disease, clear margins, and a
patient willing to commit to endocrine therapy, whole-breast irradiation was presented as
optional: it reduces in-breast recurrence but has not demonstrated a survival advantage in
this subgroup. After counselling she chose to omit radiotherapy and began anastrozole for
five years, with baseline DEXA and calcium/vitamin D supplementation given her osteopenia.
Annual mammography and six-monthly clinical review were arranged, with adherence stressed —
omitting radiotherapy is only defensible if the endocrine therapy is actually taken.

**Teaching point.** A small, low-grade, strongly ER-positive, node-negative cancer in a woman
over 70 is the specific setting in which radiotherapy may reasonably be omitted after
breast-conserving surgery — accepting a higher local recurrence rate in exchange for reduced
treatment burden, and contingent on endocrine adherence.

## Case record 2025-02-11 · 44F · palpable anterior neck nodule — THYROID, not breast

**Presentation.** A 44-year-old woman noticed a firm, painless lump in the lower
anterior neck while applying moisturizer. The mass moved on swallowing. No
hoarseness, no dysphagia, no compressive symptoms, no B symptoms. No family
history of thyroid or endocrine neoplasia; no prior neck irradiation. Bilateral
breast examination was normal and her most recent screening mammogram (BI-RADS 1)
was unremarkable — this case is **not** a breast presentation.

**Imaging.** Thyroid ultrasound showed a 1.7 cm solid hypoechoic nodule in the
right lobe with irregular margins, taller-than-wide orientation, and punctate
echogenic foci — ACR TI-RADS 5. Two subcentimetre spongiform nodules in the left
lobe were TI-RADS 2. Central compartment nodes were normal; one right level IV
lateral node showed rounded morphology and loss of the fatty hilum, raising
concern for nodal metastasis.

**Pathology.** Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration of the dominant nodule
returned Bethesda category VI, positive for malignancy, favouring papillary
thyroid carcinoma. FNA of the suspicious level IV node was also positive, with a
washout thyroglobulin far above serum. TSH was normal at 1.4 mIU/L. Note that
ER/PR/HER2 receptor testing has **no role here**; thyroid carcinoma is
characterised by histologic subtype and molecular drivers such as BRAF V600E, not
by breast biomarker panels.

**Management.** Total thyroidectomy with therapeutic right lateral and central
neck dissection. Final staging pT1bN1b, classical papillary variant, no
extrathyroidal extension, margins negative. Preoperative and postoperative
laryngoscopy documented intact vocal cord mobility. Adjuvant radioactive iodine
was discussed at the endocrine tumour board; cytotoxic adjuvant chemotherapy was
explicitly **not** indicated. Levothyroxine was started with a TSH suppression
target, and surveillance planned with serum thyroglobulin, anti-thyroglobulin
antibodies, and neck ultrasound at six months to detect recurrence.

**Teaching point:** a palpable neck lump that elevates on swallowing is a thyroid
problem, not a breast problem — TI-RADS and Bethesda drive the workup, surgery is
thyroidectomy with node dissection, and any answer invoking sentinel lymph node
biopsy, endocrine therapy for hormone receptors, or breast adjuvant chemotherapy
protocols is retrieving the wrong disease.

**Presentation.** A 63-year-old postmenopausal woman, para 2, presented with four
months of abdominal bloating, early satiety, and a 5 kg weight loss. She had been
treated for presumed irritable bowel syndrome. Examination found a distended
abdomen with shifting dullness and a fixed mass palpable on bimanual pelvic
examination. Clinical breast examination was normal and her screening mammogram
eleven months earlier was BI-RADS 1 — this record documents **no breast disease**.

with thick septations, solid mural nodules, and marked internal vascularity, plus
moderate ascites — O-RADS 5. Contrast CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed
omental caking, peritoneal implants, and bulky retroperitoneal nodes; there was no
parenchymal liver metastasis. CA-125 was 1,480 U/mL with CEA 2.1 ng/mL, and the
CA-125:CEA ratio above 25 argued against a metastatic gastrointestinal primary.

**Pathology and genetics.** Image-guided omental core biopsy showed high-grade
serous carcinoma, WT1 positive, p53 aberrant (null pattern), PAX8 positive —
a Müllerian primary. **ER weak positivity was noted immunohistochemically but is
not used to direct endocrine therapy here**, and HER2 testing was not part of the
workup. Germline and somatic testing identified a pathogenic BRCA1 variant, which
matters both for PARP inhibitor maintenance and for cascade family testing;
elevated lifetime breast cancer risk was discussed as a future screening issue,
not as the current diagnosis.

**Management.** Given extensive peritoneal disease and poor predicted resectability,
the gynaecologic oncology tumour board recommended neoadjuvant carboplatin and
paclitaxel for three cycles, followed by interval debulking surgery aiming for no
gross residual disease, then three further cycles and PARP inhibitor maintenance.
There was no role for sentinel lymph node biopsy or for any breast-directed
intervention. Response was tracked by CA-125 trend and interval CT.

**Teaching point:** bloating, early satiety, ascites, and an O-RADS 5 adnexal mass
with a high CA-125 define an ovarian cancer pathway — neoadjuvant platinum-taxane
chemotherapy and interval debulking, with BRCA1 status driving maintenance — and
the incidental ER positivity in this tumour is a lexical trap, not a reason to
retrieve this case for a hormone-receptor breast cancer question.

## Case record 2025-08-26 · 39F · 1.4 cm node-negative HER2-positive carcinoma, upfront surgery

**Presentation.** A 39-year-old premenopausal woman, fourteen months after weaning her second
child, felt a firm painless nodule in the right breast during self-examination. Cycles were
regular, there was no nipple discharge or skin change, no family history, and she had never
had prior breast imaging.

**Workup.** Ultrasound was the first-line study given her age: a 1.4 cm irregular hypoechoic
mass at the 10 o'clock position, 4 cm from the nipple, non-parallel in orientation with
posterior acoustic shadowing. Mammography in heterogeneously dense tissue confirmed an
irregular mass with a few associated coarse heterogeneous calcifications. Assessment was
BI-RADS 4C. Dedicated axillary ultrasound showed nodes with preserved fatty hila and cortical
thickness under 2 mm, so no node sampling was performed. Ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the
mass was taken with clip placement. Staging imaging beyond the breast was not indicated for
clinical stage I disease.

**Pathology.** Invasive ductal carcinoma, grade 3, ER <1% (negative), PR 0%, HER2 IHC 3+
(reflex ISH not required), Ki-67 45%, with adjacent focal high-grade DCIS.

**Course.** With a clinically node-negative sub-2 cm tumour, upfront surgery was chosen over
neoadjuvant systemic therapy — the tumour was already small enough that preoperative
treatment would not alter the surgical plan, and definitive pathological staging was
preferred. Breast-conserving surgery with sentinel node biopsy yielded a 15 mm invasive
carcinoma, closest margin 4 mm, 0/3 sentinel nodes negative — pT1c pN0. Baseline
echocardiography showed an LVEF of 62%. Adjuvant therapy was de-escalated to weekly
paclitaxel for twelve weeks with trastuzumab, continuing trastuzumab to complete one year,

counselling preceded chemotherapy and she banked oocytes. No endocrine therapy was given, as

bulky or node-positive HER2-positive disease: surgery comes first, and a single-agent taxane
with trastuzumab suffices — dual HER2 blockade, anthracyclines, and neoadjuvant sequencing
are reserved for higher-stage presentations.

## Treatment guidance (2025-02-11) · Selecting adjuvant systemic therapy in early breast cancer by receptor subtype

Scope: resected stage I–III invasive carcinoma, post-operative setting, decision about which
*class* of systemic therapy to offer. This note does not cover drug-level choices within a
class, nor the neoadjuvant setting.

**Step one is the receptor panel, not the tumour size.** ER, PR and HER2 must be reported on
adequate tissue before any systemic plan is drafted. If the core needle biopsy result is
equivocal, borderline, or based on scant tissue, repeat testing on the surgical specimen
rather than proceeding on a provisional subtype.

**Hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative.** Endocrine therapy is the backbone for nearly
every patient in this group; the real question is whether chemotherapy adds anything on top.
For node-negative tumours roughly 0.6–5.0 cm, a validated multigene recurrence assay is the
usual tie-breaker: a low genomic score generally supports endocrine therapy alone, a high
score supports adding chemotherapy. In premenopausal patients under 50 with an intermediate
score, apparent chemotherapy benefit may partly reflect chemotherapy-induced ovarian
suppression, which changes how the result should be read. With 1–3 involved nodes the assay
is informative but less decisive and the case belongs in tumour board discussion.

**ER-low disease (1–10% staining)** should not be managed as if it were robustly
hormone-driven. It behaves closer to triple-negative disease, and endocrine therapy alone is
rarely sufficient.

**HER2-positive, any hormone-receptor status.** Chemotherapy plus HER2-directed antibody
therapy is the expected backbone; regimen selection is addressed separately.

**Triple-negative.** There is no endocrine or HER2 target, so cytotoxic chemotherapy —
typically an anthracycline and taxane sequence — is the only systemic option. For tumours
2 cm or larger, or with clinically involved nodes, delivering that chemotherapy before
surgery is usually preferred so that response is measurable. Germline BRCA1/2 testing should
be arranged early, since a pathogenic variant opens an additional adjuvant option.

**Sequencing.** Chemotherapy precedes endocrine therapy; tamoxifen is not given concurrently
with cytotoxic chemotherapy. Radiotherapy planning proceeds in parallel and is not delayed
waiting for genomic results.

Treatment decisions belong to the multidisciplinary team and the patient; decision-support
tools do not prescribe.

## Treatment guidance (2025-02-11) · Selecting adjuvant systemic therapy in early breast cancer by receptor subtype

Scope: resected stage I–III invasive carcinoma, post-operative setting, decision about which
*class* of systemic therapy to offer. This note does not cover drug-level choices within a
class, nor the neoadjuvant setting.

**Step one is the receptor panel, not the tumour size.** ER, PR and HER2 must be reported on
adequate tissue before any systemic plan is drafted. If the core needle biopsy result is
equivocal, borderline, or based on scant tissue, repeat testing on the surgical specimen
rather than proceeding on a provisional subtype.

**Hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative.** Endocrine therapy is the backbone for nearly
every patient in this group; the real question is whether chemotherapy adds anything on top.
For node-negative tumours roughly 0.6–5.0 cm, a validated multigene recurrence assay is the
usual tie-breaker: a low genomic score generally supports endocrine therapy alone, a high
score supports adding chemotherapy. In premenopausal patients under 50 with an intermediate
score, apparent chemotherapy benefit may partly reflect chemotherapy-induced ovarian
suppression, which changes how the result should be read. With 1–3 involved nodes the assay
is informative but less decisive and the case belongs in tumour board discussion.

**ER-low disease (1–10% staining)** should not be managed as if it were robustly
hormone-driven. It behaves closer to triple-negative disease, and endocrine therapy alone is
rarely sufficient.

**HER2-positive, any hormone-receptor status.** Chemotherapy plus HER2-directed antibody
therapy is the expected backbone; regimen selection is addressed separately.

**Triple-negative.** There is no endocrine or HER2 target, so cytotoxic chemotherapy —
typically an anthracycline and taxane sequence — is the only systemic option. For tumours
2 cm or larger, or with clinically involved nodes, delivering that chemotherapy before
surgery is usually preferred so that response is measurable. Germline BRCA1/2 testing should
be arranged early, since a pathogenic variant opens an additional adjuvant option.

**Sequencing.** Chemotherapy precedes endocrine therapy; tamoxifen is not given concurrently
with cytotoxic chemotherapy. Radiotherapy planning proceeds in parallel and is not delayed
waiting for genomic results.

tools do not prescribe.

## Treatment guidance (2025-09-30) · Neoadjuvant therapy: patient selection and assessment of response

Scope: systemic therapy delivered before surgery in non-metastatic disease. This note covers
who should be offered it and how response is judged. It does not cover choice of individual
cytotoxic agents.

**Two separate reasons to treat before operating.** The first is surgical: a large tumour in a
patient who wants breast conservation, or bulky nodal disease, may become operable or
conservable after downstaging. The second, and increasingly the more important, is
informational — the response of the tumour to chemotherapy is a strong prognostic signal, and
in triple-negative and HER2-positive disease that signal directly changes what is given after
surgery. A patient with residual disease can be offered escalated post-operative treatment
that would never have been identified had they gone straight to theatre.

**Who is a candidate.** Triple-negative and HER2-positive tumours of roughly 2 cm or larger,
or with clinically involved nodes, are the clearest candidates. Inflammatory breast cancer is
always treated systemically first. By contrast, strongly hormone-receptor-positive,
HER2-negative, low-grade tumours respond poorly to chemotherapy and rarely achieve a complete
response, so pre-operative chemotherapy is usually not the right tool for them; upfront
surgery is generally preferred unless downstaging is specifically needed.

**Before the first cycle.** Establish histological diagnosis with a core needle biopsy —
never fine-needle aspiration alone — with full receptor and HER2 testing. Place a radiopaque
marker clip in the tumour bed and in any biopsy-proven abnormal node, because a complete
response can erase the target and leave the surgeon nothing to excise. Baseline imaging should
be documented, and staging investigations completed for stage III or clinically suspicious
presentations.

**Assessing response.** Clinical examination and imaging are used mid-treatment mainly to
detect progression, which mandates re-evaluation of the plan; they do not reliably predict
the final pathological result. MRI correlates better than mammography but still over- and
under-estimates residual disease. The definitive endpoint is pathology at surgery: a
pathological complete response means no residual invasive carcinoma in the breast and no
nodal involvement, with residual DCIS still counted as a complete response by the usual
convention. Residual disease should be quantified in a structured way and reported to the
tumour board, since it determines post-operative escalation.

tools do not prescribe.

# SYNTHETIC — invented for demo purposes. Not a real patient and not a real guideline.

## Diagnostic guidance (2025-11) · Referral for genetic counselling and germline testing

Scope: which breast clinic patients should be referred for hereditary cancer counselling
and germline testing, and what the result changes. This concerns inherited variants in
blood or saliva. It does not cover somatic tumor sequencing, and it does not cover
multigene prognostic assays used to decide adjuvant chemotherapy.

1. Counselling precedes testing and follows it. The pre-test conversation covers what a
   result would change, implications for relatives, and reproductive and insurance
   consequences; the post-test conversation translates the report into management.
2. Refer any patient diagnosed with breast cancer at or under 45 years, irrespective of
   family history.
3. Refer a diagnosis at or under 50 when there is also a close relative with breast,
   ovarian, pancreatic, or high-risk prostate cancer, or when the patient has had a
   second primary breast cancer.
4. Refer triple-negative breast cancer diagnosed up to about age 60 regardless of family
   history; the yield of a BRCA1 variant in this group is high enough to justify testing
   on histology alone.
5. Refer every male breast cancer, at any age.
6. Refer bilateral disease, particularly when the first primary occurred before
   menopause.
7. Refer on family structure: two or more close relatives on the same side of the family
   with breast cancer, any relative with ovarian carcinoma, a constellation of breast
   with pancreatic or metastatic prostate cancer, or Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry with any
   affected relative.
8. When a pathogenic variant is already known in the family, test the patient for that
   specific variant first. A broad panel is unnecessary and complicates interpretation.
9. Invasive lobular carcinoma with a family history of diffuse gastric cancer should
   prompt consideration of CDH1.
10. Panels typically report high-penetrance genes including BRCA1, BRCA2, and PALB2;
    moderate-penetrance genes such as ATM and CHEK2; and syndromic genes including TP53,
    PTEN, and STK11. Penetrance differs enormously between these tiers and management
    must follow the tier, not merely the presence of a name on the report.
11. A pathogenic result changes real decisions: it reframes the discussion of
    contralateral risk-reducing mastectomy, prompts risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy
    for BRCA carriers, supports annual MRI surveillance, may open PARP inhibitor
    eligibility, and enables cascade testing of relatives.
12. A variant of uncertain significance is not actionable. Never plan surgery on a VUS.
13. A negative panel in a patient with a strong family history does not return her to
    average risk; her empiric risk still comes from the pedigree.

Refer triple-negative breast cancer diagnosed up to about age 60 regardless of family history; the yield of a BRCA1 variant in this group is high enough to justify testing on histology alone [2025-11-12_guide_dx_genetic_counselling_referral.md].

## Case record 2025-12-03 · 63F · complex adnexal mass and ascites — OVARIAN, not breast

**Presentation.** A 63-year-old postmenopausal woman, para 2, presented with four
months of abdominal bloating, early satiety, and a 5 kg weight loss. She had been
treated for presumed irritable bowel syndrome. Examination found a distended
abdomen with shifting dullness and a fixed mass palpable on bimanual pelvic
examination. Clinical breast examination was normal and her screening mammogram
eleven months earlier was BI-RADS 1 — this record documents **no breast disease**.

**Imaging and markers.** Transvaginal ultrasound showed a 9 cm right adnexal mass
with thick septations, solid mural nodules, and marked internal vascularity, plus
moderate ascites — O-RADS 5. Contrast CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed
omental caking, peritoneal implants, and bulky retroperitoneal nodes; there was no
parenchymal liver metastasis. CA-125 was 1,480 U/mL with CEA 2.1 ng/mL, and the
CA-125:CEA ratio above 25 argued against a metastatic gastrointestinal primary.

**Pathology and genetics.** Image-guided omental core biopsy showed high-grade
serous carcinoma, WT1 positive, p53 aberrant (null pattern), PAX8 positive —
a Müllerian primary. **ER weak positivity was noted immunohistochemically but is
not used to direct endocrine therapy here**, and HER2 testing was not part of the
workup. Germline and somatic testing identified a pathogenic BRCA1 variant, which
matters both for PARP inhibitor maintenance and for cascade family testing;
elevated lifetime breast cancer risk was discussed as a future screening issue,
not as the current diagnosis.

**Management.** Given extensive peritoneal disease and poor predicted resectability,
the gynaecologic oncology tumour board recommended neoadjuvant carboplatin and
paclitaxel for three cycles, followed by interval debulking surgery aiming for no
gross residual disease, then three further cycles and PARP inhibitor maintenance.
There was no role for sentinel lymph node biopsy or for any breast-directed
intervention. Response was tracked by CA-125 trend and interval CT.

**Teaching point:** bloating, early satiety, ascites, and an O-RADS 5 adnexal mass
with a high CA-125 define an ovarian cancer pathway — neoadjuvant platinum-taxane
chemotherapy and interval debulking, with BRCA1 status driving maintenance — and
the incidental ER positivity in this tumour is a lexical trap, not a reason to
retrieve this case for a hormone-receptor breast cancer question.

For a patient with an O-RADS 5 adnexal mass, extensive peritoneal disease, and poor predicted resectability, the recommended management was neoadjuvant carboplatin and paclitaxel for three cycles, followed by interval debulking surgery, three further chemotherapy cycles, and PARP inhibitor maintenance [2025-12-03_case_other_ovarian_mass_workup_63F.md].

## Case record 2025-02-11 · 44F · palpable anterior neck nodule — THYROID, not breast

**Presentation.** A 44-year-old woman noticed a firm, painless lump in the lower
anterior neck while applying moisturizer. The mass moved on swallowing. No
hoarseness, no dysphagia, no compressive symptoms, no B symptoms. No family
history of thyroid or endocrine neoplasia; no prior neck irradiation. Bilateral
breast examination was normal and her most recent screening mammogram (BI-RADS 1)
was unremarkable — this case is **not** a breast presentation.

**Imaging.** Thyroid ultrasound showed a 1.7 cm solid hypoechoic nodule in the
right lobe with irregular margins, taller-than-wide orientation, and punctate
echogenic foci — ACR TI-RADS 5. Two subcentimetre spongiform nodules in the left
lobe were TI-RADS 2. Central compartment nodes were normal; one right level IV
lateral node showed rounded morphology and loss of the fatty hilum, raising
concern for nodal metastasis.

**Pathology.** Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration of the dominant nodule
returned Bethesda category VI, positive for malignancy, favouring papillary
thyroid carcinoma. FNA of the suspicious level IV node was also positive, with a
washout thyroglobulin far above serum. TSH was normal at 1.4 mIU/L. Note that
ER/PR/HER2 receptor testing has **no role here**; thyroid carcinoma is
characterised by histologic subtype and molecular drivers such as BRAF V600E, not
by breast biomarker panels.

**Management.** Total thyroidectomy with therapeutic right lateral and central
neck dissection. Final staging pT1bN1b, classical papillary variant, no
extrathyroidal extension, margins negative. Preoperative and postoperative
laryngoscopy documented intact vocal cord mobility. Adjuvant radioactive iodine
was discussed at the endocrine tumour board; cytotoxic adjuvant chemotherapy was
explicitly **not** indicated. Levothyroxine was started with a TSH suppression
target, and surveillance planned with serum thyroglobulin, anti-thyroglobulin
antibodies, and neck ultrasound at six months to detect recurrence.

problem, not a breast problem — TI-RADS and Bethesda drive the workup, surgery is
thyroidectomy with node dissection, and any answer invoking sentinel lymph node

## Case record 2025-04-08 · 44F · supraclavicular and internal mammary nodal recurrence, 20 months after HER2-directed therapy

**Presentation.** A 44-year-old premenopausal woman presented with three weeks of painless
fullness in the left supraclavicular fossa and new heaviness of the left arm. Twenty months
earlier she had completed treatment for left-sided HER2-positive breast cancer: neoadjuvant
dose-dense doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide followed by paclitaxel with trastuzumab and pertuzumab,
then left mastectomy with axillary dissection showing residual disease (ypT2 ypN2a), followed by
14 cycles of adjuvant T-DM1 and post-mastectomy radiotherapy to the chest wall and axilla. The
original tumor was ER 0%, PR 0%, HER2 IHC 3+.

**Restaging workup.** Ultrasound showed a 2.4 cm rounded left supraclavicular node with absent
fatty hilum, plus two smaller level IV nodes. FDG PET/CT demonstrated avid left supraclavicular
and left internal mammary nodes, with no pulmonary, hepatic, or skeletal uptake. Contrast MRI of
the brain was performed because of the HER2-positive phenotype and was negative. Echocardiography
showed LVEF 58%.

**Biopsy confirmation.** Ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the supraclavicular node returned
metastatic carcinoma of breast origin, ER 0%, PR 0%, HER2 IHC 3+ — concordant with the primary
and confirming persistent HER2-driven biology despite prior trastuzumab, pertuzumab, and T-DM1.

**Management decision.** Because the internal mammary and supraclavicular basins are regional,
this was staged as recurrent locoregional (stage IIIC-equivalent) disease rather than M1, and the
board pursued aggressive multimodality control. Given relapse on adjuvant T-DM1, the disease was
considered T-DM1-refractory, and systemic therapy began with trastuzumab deruxtecan. Radiation
oncology reviewed the prior treatment plan and dose-volume histograms; the supraclavicular fossa
lay at the field edge, so re-irradiation was judged feasible after maximal systemic response, with
surgical nodal clearance reserved for residual disease. Ovarian function preservation counseling
and a repeat germline panel were arranged.

**Teaching point.** This differs from a first presentation in that the relapse interval itself is
the key datum: recurrence 20 months after completing HER2-directed therapy defines
treatment-refractory biology and moves the patient past first-line anti-HER2 options. It also
differs from an isolated axillary recurrence — supraclavicular and internal mammary involvement
demands re-irradiation planning against a prior dose map rather than straightforward dissection.

The multidisciplinary board treated this as recurrent locoregional (stage IIIC-equivalent) disease rather than M1, and pursued aggressive multimodality curative intent. (2025-04-08_case_adv_supraclavicular_nodal_recurrence_44F.md)

## Diagnostic guidance (2025-02) · Workup of a new discrete palpable breast mass

Scope: the first diagnostic encounter for an adult presenting with a new, discrete,
palpable lump. This document does not cover asymptomatic screening intervals, nipple
discharge without a mass, or post-treatment surveillance imaging.

1. Triple assessment means three concurrent legs — clinical examination, targeted
   imaging, and tissue sampling when indicated. A lump is not cleared until all
   applicable legs agree.

   ultrasound of the palpable site; add mammography only if ultrasound is suspicious

## Case record 2025-10-14 · 51M · pigmented back lesion with sentinel node biopsy — MELANOMA, not breast

**Presentation.** A 51-year-old man with fair skin and a history of blistering
sunburns was referred after his partner noticed a changing mole on the left upper
back. Over eight months it had darkened, developed an irregular notched border,
and intermittently bled after towel drying. Dermoscopy showed an atypical
pigment network with blue-white veil and irregular globules. Examination of the
chest wall and both axillae was otherwise normal; there is **no breast lesion**
in this record, only a cutaneous one.

**Pathology.** Excisional biopsy with 2 mm margins showed superficial spreading
melanoma, Breslow thickness 2.3 mm, no ulceration, mitotic rate 3/mm², clear
peripheral and deep margins on the diagnostic excision. Staging was pT3a.
Immunohistochemistry used SOX10 and Melan-A; **ER, PR, and HER2 were not tested**
and have no role in melanoma. BRAF V600E mutation testing was positive, which is
what actually determines targeted systemic options here.

**Nodal staging.** Because Breslow thickness exceeded 1 mm, lymphoscintigraphy
and sentinel lymph node biopsy were offered. Technetium-99m colloid injected
intradermally around the biopsy scar mapped to the **left axilla**, and two
sentinel nodes were harvested. One node contained a 0.4 mm subcapsular deposit of
melanoma. Note that a positive axillary sentinel node here reflects drainage from
the back skin, not from breast parenchyma — the anatomy is shared, the disease is
not. Completion axillary dissection was **not** performed; current practice
favours nodal ultrasound surveillance after a positive sentinel node in melanoma.

**Management.** Wide local excision of the primary site was completed with 2 cm
margins. Staging CT and brain MRI showed no distant metastasis, giving stage IIIA
disease. Adjuvant anti-PD-1 immunotherapy was recommended for one year; cytotoxic
adjuvant chemotherapy was **not** offered, as it is ineffective in this setting.
Follow-up included skin surveillance every three months and axillary ultrasound.

**Teaching point:** sentinel lymph node biopsy draining to the axilla is not
unique to breast cancer — in cutaneous melanoma it follows Breslow thickness,
completion dissection is avoided, and adjuvant therapy is checkpoint blockade
guided by BRAF status, so retrieving this case for a breast SLNB question is a
clear error.

## Case record 2025-01-27 · 29F · lactational mastitis progressing to breast abscess

**Presentation.** A 29-year-old woman, five weeks postpartum and exclusively
breastfeeding, presented with two days of left breast pain, a hard tender area, fever to
38.6 °C, and flu-like aching. She reported difficulty with latch on the left and a
recently missed night feed. No trauma, no prior breast disease.

**Examination.** A wedge-shaped area of erythema, warmth, and induration over the left
upper outer quadrant, exquisitely tender, with a cracked nipple. Mildly tender reactive
left axillary node. No skin ulceration, no nipple retraction, no orange-peel change over
the whole breast.

**Initial management.** Diagnosed clinically as lactational mastitis. Treated with
effective milk removal (continued breastfeeding on the affected side plus expression),
analgesia, and oral cephalexin covering *Staphylococcus aureus*. Breastfeeding was
explicitly encouraged, not stopped.

**Escalation.** At 72 hours the fever persisted and a fluctuant area developed. Ultrasound
showed a 3.6 cm collection with thick irregular walls, internal debris and swirling echoes
on compression, and peripheral hyperaemia — a **lactational breast abscess**.
Ultrasound-guided needle aspiration drained 22 mL of purulent fluid; the catheter-free
aspiration was repeated once at 48 hours. Culture grew methicillin-sensitive *S. aureus*
sensitive to the prescribed agent. Surgical incision and drainage was avoided.

**Features pointing away from malignancy.** The context of lactation; acute onset over
days with systemic fever; a cracked nipple as a portal of entry; localised wedge-shaped
rather than whole-breast erythema; positive culture; and, most important, prompt and
complete clinical resolution once drained and treated.

**Red flags that would have changed the plan.** Inflammatory breast carcinoma is the
diagnosis that must not be missed. Warning features would have been: a non-lactating or
postmenopausal patient; erythema involving more than one third of the breast with peau
d'orange and no fever; failure of the inflammation to resolve after an adequate course of
antibiotics and drainage; a persistent underlying mass after resolution; matted or fixed
axillary nodes. Any of these mandates full-thickness skin punch biopsy plus core needle
biopsy of the breast parenchyma, not another antibiotic course.

**Course.** Afebrile by day 6; erythema resolved by day 12; breastfeeding continued
throughout. Follow-up ultrasound at 6 weeks showed no residual collection and no
underlying mass.

Teaching point: a lactating woman with fever and focal erythema has mastitis until an
abscess is found — but inflammation that does not clear after adequate treatment must be
biopsied to exclude inflammatory breast carcinoma.

## Treatment guidance (2025-09-30) · Neoadjuvant therapy: patient selection and assessment of response

Scope: systemic therapy delivered before surgery in non-metastatic disease. This note covers
who should be offered it and how response is judged. It does not cover choice of individual
cytotoxic agents.

**Two separate reasons to treat before operating.** The first is surgical: a large tumour in a
patient who wants breast conservation, or bulky nodal disease, may become operable or
conservable after downstaging. The second, and increasingly the more important, is
informational — the response of the tumour to chemotherapy is a strong prognostic signal, and
in triple-negative and HER2-positive disease that signal directly changes what is given after
surgery. A patient with residual disease can be offered escalated post-operative treatment
that would never have been identified had they gone straight to theatre.

**Who is a candidate.** Triple-negative and HER2-positive tumours of roughly 2 cm or larger,
or with clinically involved nodes, are the clearest candidates. Inflammatory breast cancer is
always treated systemically first. By contrast, strongly hormone-receptor-positive,
HER2-negative, low-grade tumours respond poorly to chemotherapy and rarely achieve a complete
response, so pre-operative chemotherapy is usually not the right tool for them; upfront
surgery is generally preferred unless downstaging is specifically needed.

**Before the first cycle.** Establish histological diagnosis with a core needle biopsy —
never fine-needle aspiration alone — with full receptor and HER2 testing. Place a radiopaque
marker clip in the tumour bed and in any biopsy-proven abnormal node, because a complete
response can erase the target and leave the surgeon nothing to excise. Baseline imaging should
be documented, and staging investigations completed for stage III or clinically suspicious
presentations.

**Assessing response.** Clinical examination and imaging are used mid-treatment mainly to
detect progression, which mandates re-evaluation of the plan; they do not reliably predict
the final pathological result. MRI correlates better than mammography but still over- and
under-estimates residual disease. The definitive endpoint is pathology at surgery: a
pathological complete response means no residual invasive carcinoma in the breast and no
nodal involvement, with residual DCIS still counted as a complete response by the usual
convention. Residual disease should be quantified in a structured way and reported to the
tumour board, since it determines post-operative escalation.

Treatment decisions belong to the multidisciplinary team and the patient; decision-support
tools do not prescribe.

## Case record 2025-08-26 · 39F · 1.4 cm node-negative HER2-positive carcinoma, upfront surgery

**Presentation.** A 39-year-old premenopausal woman, fourteen months after weaning her second
child, felt a firm painless nodule in the right breast during self-examination. Cycles were
regular, there was no nipple discharge or skin change, no family history, and she had never
had prior breast imaging.

**Workup.** Ultrasound was the first-line study given her age: a 1.4 cm irregular hypoechoic
mass at the 10 o'clock position, 4 cm from the nipple, non-parallel in orientation with
posterior acoustic shadowing. Mammography in heterogeneously dense tissue confirmed an
irregular mass with a few associated coarse heterogeneous calcifications. Assessment was
BI-RADS 4C. Dedicated axillary ultrasound showed nodes with preserved fatty hila and cortical
thickness under 2 mm, so no node sampling was performed. Ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the
mass was taken with clip placement. Staging imaging beyond the breast was not indicated for
clinical stage I disease.

**Pathology.** Invasive ductal carcinoma, grade 3, ER <1% (negative), PR 0%, HER2 IHC 3+
(reflex ISH not required), Ki-67 45%, with adjacent focal high-grade DCIS.

**Course.** With a clinically node-negative sub-2 cm tumour, upfront surgery was chosen over
neoadjuvant systemic therapy — the tumour was already small enough that preoperative
treatment would not alter the surgical plan, and definitive pathological staging was
preferred. Breast-conserving surgery with sentinel node biopsy yielded a 15 mm invasive
carcinoma, closest margin 4 mm, 0/3 sentinel nodes negative — pT1c pN0. Baseline
echocardiography showed an LVEF of 62%. Adjuvant therapy was de-escalated to weekly
paclitaxel for twelve weeks with trastuzumab, continuing trastuzumab to complete one year,
in place of an anthracycline-containing regimen. Whole-breast radiotherapy with a tumour-bed
boost followed chemotherapy. Cardiac function was reassessed every three months. Fertility
counselling preceded chemotherapy and she banked oocytes. No endocrine therapy was given, as
the tumour was hormone-receptor negative.

**Teaching point.** Small node-negative HER2-positive disease is handled very differently from
bulky or node-positive HER2-positive disease: surgery comes first, and a single-agent taxane
with trastuzumab suffices — dual HER2 blockade, anthracyclines, and neoadjuvant sequencing
are reserved for higher-stage presentations.

## Case record 2025-10-13 · 58F · mammographically occult invasive lobular carcinoma, node-positive

**Presentation.** A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman described a persistent area of altered
texture in the upper outer left breast over about five months, without a lump she could
outline and without skin or nipple change. She had used menopausal hormone therapy for four
years, stopping at age 55. Examination found a firm, ill-defined region of thickening roughly
4 cm across with no palpable mass edge and no axillary node palpable.

**Workup.** Mammography showed extremely dense tissue with a subtle developing asymmetry in
the left upper outer quadrant and no calcifications; the study was initially assessed BI-RADS 0
pending ultrasound. Ultrasound found a 2.1 cm ill-defined hypoechoic area with marked
posterior shadowing, poorly separable from surrounding parenchyma, plus two level I axillary
nodes with cortical thickening to 5 mm and loss of the fatty hilum — assessed BI-RADS 5.
Core biopsy of the breast lesion and fine-needle aspiration of a node were performed. Breast
MRI was obtained because clinical extent exceeded the sonographic finding, and showed 5.8 cm
of non-mass enhancement with two satellite foci in separate quadrants.

**Pathology.** Invasive lobular carcinoma, classic type, with single-file infiltration and
absent membranous E-cadherin on immunohistochemistry. Grade 2, ER 100%, PR 70%, HER2 IHC 0,
Ki-67 12%. Node aspirate positive for carcinoma.

**Course.** Multicentric disease across quadrants excluded breast conservation, and total
mastectomy was performed. Sentinel mapping retrieved four nodes, three containing
macrometastases, so completion axillary lymph node dissection followed; two of a further
twelve nodes were positive, giving five positive nodes overall. The largest invasive focus
measured 3.4 cm — pT2 pN2a. Genomic recurrence assays were not pursued given the nodal
burden. She received adjuvant anthracycline followed by taxane chemotherapy, then
post-mastectomy radiotherapy to the chest wall with supraclavicular and internal mammary
coverage, then letrozole with extended endocrine therapy planned beyond five years.

**Teaching point.** Invasive lobular carcinoma consistently under-declares its size on
mammography and ultrasound; when clinical extent outruns the imaging, preoperative MRI
changes the operation — here from attempted conservation to mastectomy — and lobular
histology should lower the threshold for obtaining it.

## Case record 2025-02-19 · 58F · isolated chest-wall recurrence 6.5 years after mastectomy

**Presentation.** A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman was referred from surveillance clinic with
two firm, non-tender pink nodules in the right mastectomy scar, measuring 6 mm and 9 mm, noticed
over roughly eight weeks. Her primary disease, treated 6.5 years earlier, was a grade 2 invasive
ductal carcinoma (IDC), pT2 pN1a (2 of 14 nodes), ER 90%, PR 60%, HER2 IHC 0, Ki-67 12%. She
underwent right total mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection, adjuvant
docetaxel/cyclophosphamide, and five years of anastrozole. Post-mastectomy radiotherapy was
discussed at the original tumor board and not delivered. She has been off all systemic therapy
for 18 months. No bone pain, no dyspnea, no weight loss.

**Restaging workup.** Chest-wall ultrasound showed two hypoechoic dermal-subdermal nodules
without deep pectoral invasion. Contralateral mammography was BI-RADS 1. Staging FDG PET/CT
demonstrated uptake confined to the two cutaneous nodules, with no internal mammary,
supraclavicular, visceral, or skeletal uptake. Liver function tests, calcium, and alkaline
phosphatase were normal.

**Biopsy confirmation.** Punch biopsy of the larger nodule returned invasive carcinoma
morphologically matching the archived primary: ER 85%, PR 30%, HER2 IHC 0. Receptor profile was
therefore concordant with the primary, and no change of biologic class was implied.

**Management decision.** The multidisciplinary board treated this as an isolated locoregional
recurrence with curative intent, not as metastatic disease. Plan: wide local excision of both
nodules to negative margins, followed by chest-wall and supraclavicular radiotherapy — feasible
because the chest wall had never been irradiated. Because the recurrence is strongly
hormone-receptor positive, systemic management was a switch of endocrine class rather than
cytotoxic therapy; she began fulvestrant with a CDK4/6 inhibitor after cardiology and bone-density
baselines. Chemotherapy was explicitly not recommended, as its benefit in resected locoregional
recurrence is concentrated in hormone-receptor-negative disease.

**Teaching point.** Unlike a first presentation, where staging establishes biology from an
untreated primary, this decision turned on what she had already received: the absence of prior
chest-wall radiotherapy made curative-intent local therapy possible, and prior aromatase
inhibitor exposure dictated the endocrine switch. An isolated chest-wall recurrence is a
potentially curable event and must not be managed as stage IV disease.

## Case record 2025-12-03 · 63F · complex adnexal mass and ascites — OVARIAN, not breast

**Presentation.** A 63-year-old postmenopausal woman, para 2, presented with four
months of abdominal bloating, early satiety, and a 5 kg weight loss. She had been
treated for presumed irritable bowel syndrome. Examination found a distended
abdomen with shifting dullness and a fixed mass palpable on bimanual pelvic
examination. Clinical breast examination was normal and her screening mammogram
eleven months earlier was BI-RADS 1 — this record documents **no breast disease**.

**Imaging and markers.** Transvaginal ultrasound showed a 9 cm right adnexal mass
with thick septations, solid mural nodules, and marked internal vascularity, plus
moderate ascites — O-RADS 5. Contrast CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed
omental caking, peritoneal implants, and bulky retroperitoneal nodes; there was no
parenchymal liver metastasis. CA-125 was 1,480 U/mL with CEA 2.1 ng/mL, and the
CA-125:CEA ratio above 25 argued against a metastatic gastrointestinal primary.

**Pathology and genetics.** Image-guided omental core biopsy showed high-grade
serous carcinoma, WT1 positive, p53 aberrant (null pattern), PAX8 positive —
a Müllerian primary. **ER weak positivity was noted immunohistochemically but is
not used to direct endocrine therapy here**, and HER2 testing was not part of the
workup. Germline and somatic testing identified a pathogenic BRCA1 variant, which
matters both for PARP inhibitor maintenance and for cascade family testing;
elevated lifetime breast cancer risk was discussed as a future screening issue,
not as the current diagnosis.

**Management.** Given extensive peritoneal disease and poor predicted resectability,
the gynaecologic oncology tumour board recommended neoadjuvant carboplatin and
paclitaxel for three cycles, followed by interval debulking surgery aiming for no
gross residual disease, then three further cycles and PARP inhibitor maintenance.
There was no role for sentinel lymph node biopsy or for any breast-directed
intervention. Response was tracked by CA-125 trend and interval CT.

**Teaching point:** bloating, early satiety, ascites, and an O-RADS 5 adnexal mass
with a high CA-125 define an ovarian cancer pathway — neoadjuvant platinum-taxane
chemotherapy and interval debulking, with BRCA1 status driving maintenance — and
the incidental ER positivity in this tumour is a lexical trap, not a reason to
retrieve this case for a hormone-receptor breast cancer question.

## Diagnostic guidance (2025-09) · Nipple discharge — separating physiologic from pathologic

Scope: nipple discharge as the presenting complaint. The task is to sort discharge into
physiologic, endocrine, or pathologic before ordering anything. Evaluation of a
palpable mass and screening of asymptomatic women are covered elsewhere.

1. Characterize the discharge on six axes: spontaneous or only expressed; unilateral
   or bilateral; single duct orifice or multiple; color and consistency; presence of an
   associated mass or skin change; and the patient's age. These six answers determine
   the pathway.
2. Physiologic discharge is bilateral, arises from multiple duct orifices, appears only
   on expression, and is milky, yellow, green, or brown-grey. It is benign, frequently
   perpetuated by repeated self-expression, and needs no imaging beyond age-appropriate
   screening. Advise the patient to stop squeezing the nipple.
3. True galactorrhea — milky discharge in a woman who is neither pregnant nor recently
   lactating — is an endocrine problem, not a breast-imaging problem. Check serum
   prolactin, TSH, and a pregnancy test, and review medications that raise prolactin,
   including antipsychotics, metoclopramide, and opioids. Persistent hyperprolactinemia
   without a drug cause warrants pituitary MRI.
4. Pathologic discharge is spontaneous, unilateral, from a single duct, and clear,
   serous, serosanguineous, or frankly bloody. Any discharge meeting this description
   requires imaging regardless of how well the patient looks.
5. Image pathologic discharge with ultrasound focused on the retroareolar ducts, plus
   diagnostic mammography in patients aged 30 and over. Under 30, start with ultrasound
   and add mammography if ultrasound is abnormal.
6. If conventional imaging is negative but the discharge is convincingly pathologic,
   contrast-enhanced breast MRI is the next step; in most centers it has displaced
   galactography for localizing an occult intraductal lesion.
7. The commonest cause of pathologic discharge is a solitary intraductal papilloma,
   followed by duct ectasia. A minority represent DCIS or invasive carcinoma, and that
   minority rises with age.
8. Cytology of the discharge fluid has poor sensitivity. A negative smear never excludes
   malignancy and should not be used to close the episode.
9. Purulent discharge with periareolar inflammation, typically in a smoker, is
   periductal mastitis or abscess. Treat it as infection and reassess the duct system
   after the inflammation settles.
10. Persistent pathologic discharge with negative imaging is an indication for surgical
    duct excision — microdochectomy for a single identified duct, central duct excision
    in older patients with multi-duct disease. Counsel that excision may end the ability
    to breastfeed on that side.

## Case record 2025-06-19 · 44F · cyclical mastalgia with focal nodularity, imaging performed

**Presentation.** A 44-year-old perimenopausal woman described 14 months of bilateral
breast heaviness and soreness beginning 7–10 days before menses and easing within two days
of onset of bleeding. Cycles had become irregular over the past year. She was not on
hormone therapy or combined oral contraception. The distinguishing feature from ordinary
cyclical pain was a persistent area of lumpiness in the left upper outer quadrant that she
could feel throughout the cycle.

**Examination.** Diffuse bilateral tenderness. In the left upper outer quadrant there was
an ill-defined region of granular nodularity roughly 4 cm across without a discrete
dominant mass, with no skin tethering and no nipple change. Axillae clear.

**Why imaging was performed here.** Unlike a woman in her twenties with purely bilateral
cyclical pain and a normal examination, this patient had two features that lowered the
threshold for imaging: age over 40 and a palpable focal abnormality that persisted across
the cycle. Bilateral digital mammography showed heterogeneously dense parenchyma
(category C) with no mass, distortion, or suspicious calcification. Targeted ultrasound of
the palpable area showed clustered microcysts and mild ductal ectasia consistent with
fibrocystic change, no solid nodule, no shadowing. Combined assessment: **BI-RADS 2.**

**Features pointing away from malignancy.** Bilaterality; strict temporal coupling to the
luteal phase with resolution after menstruation; nodularity that was granular and diffuse
rather than a discrete dominant mass; no skin or nipple change; and concordant negative
mammography plus ultrasound in a symptomatic quadrant.

**Red flags that would have changed the plan.** Pain that was unilateral, fixed to one
point, non-cyclical and progressive; a discrete dominant mass within the nodular area;
spontaneous unilateral serosanguineous nipple discharge; skin thickening or peau d'orange;
new nipple inversion; or a suspicious sonographic correlate. Any of these would have
required core needle biopsy of the focal lesion, regardless of the pain pattern.

**Course.** Managed with a properly fitted supportive bra, topical diclofenac to the
tender areas during the luteal phase, and a symptom diary over three cycles. Pain score
fell from 7/10 to 3/10. No endocrine agent (danazol or tamoxifen) was needed. Reviewed at
6 months, unchanged.

Teaching point: cyclical mastalgia is benign, but focal persistent nodularity in a woman
over 40 earns imaging — the pain is reassuring, the lump is what must be cleared.

## Treatment guidance (2025-09-30) · Neoadjuvant therapy: patient selection and assessment of response

Scope: systemic therapy delivered before surgery in non-metastatic disease. This note covers
who should be offered it and how response is judged. It does not cover choice of individual
cytotoxic agents.

**Two separate reasons to treat before operating.** The first is surgical: a large tumour in a
patient who wants breast conservation, or bulky nodal disease, may become operable or
conservable after downstaging. The second, and increasingly the more important, is
informational — the response of the tumour to chemotherapy is a strong prognostic signal, and
in triple-negative and HER2-positive disease that signal directly changes what is given after
surgery. A patient with residual disease can be offered escalated post-operative treatment
that would never have been identified had they gone straight to theatre.

**Who is a candidate.** Triple-negative and HER2-positive tumours of roughly 2 cm or larger,
or with clinically involved nodes, are the clearest candidates. Inflammatory breast cancer is
always treated systemically first. By contrast, strongly hormone-receptor-positive,
HER2-negative, low-grade tumours respond poorly to chemotherapy and rarely achieve a complete
response, so pre-operative chemotherapy is usually not the right tool for them; upfront
surgery is generally preferred unless downstaging is specifically needed.

**Before the first cycle.** Establish histological diagnosis with a core needle biopsy —
never fine-needle aspiration alone — with full receptor and HER2 testing. Place a radiopaque
marker clip in the tumour bed and in any biopsy-proven abnormal node, because a complete
response can erase the target and leave the surgeon nothing to excise. Baseline imaging should
be documented, and staging investigations completed for stage III or clinically suspicious
presentations.

**Assessing response.** Clinical examination and imaging are used mid-treatment mainly to
detect progression, which mandates re-evaluation of the plan; they do not reliably predict
the final pathological result. MRI correlates better than mammography but still over- and
under-estimates residual disease. The definitive endpoint is pathology at surgery: a
pathological complete response means no residual invasive carcinoma in the breast and no
nodal involvement, with residual DCIS still counted as a complete response by the usual
convention. Residual disease should be quantified in a structured way and reported to the
tumour board, since it determines post-operative escalation.

Treatment decisions belong to the multidisciplinary team and the patient; decision-support
tools do not prescribe.

## Treatment guidance (2025-05-06) · Endocrine therapy: the tamoxifen versus aromatase-inhibitor decision

Scope: adjuvant endocrine therapy for hormone-receptor-positive invasive breast cancer. This
note covers only the choice between a selective estrogen receptor modulator and an aromatase
inhibitor, and the information required before that choice can be made.

**Menopausal status is a required input, not a refinement.** The two drug classes work by
different mechanisms, and the mechanism of one of them fails outright in the wrong patient.
Tamoxifen blocks the estrogen receptor and works regardless of where estrogen comes from.
Aromatase inhibitors — anastrozole, letrozole, exemestane — work by blocking peripheral
conversion of androgens to estrogen, which is the dominant source of estrogen only after the
ovaries have stopped producing it. Given alone to a patient with functioning ovaries, an
aromatase inhibitor does not adequately suppress estrogen and can provoke reflex ovarian
stimulation. Prescribing one without established menopausal status is therefore not a
cautious approximation; it is a potentially ineffective treatment.

**Consequently, an endocrine regimen cannot be selected from receptor status alone.** If a
request specifies "ER-positive, start endocrine therapy" without menopausal status, the
correct response is to decline to name an agent and to ask for the missing information. The
same applies when menopausal status is merely assumed from age: a 49-year-old may be
premenopausal or postmenopausal, and chemotherapy-induced amenorrhoea is not proof of
menopause because ovarian function can recover.

**Once status is established.** Premenopausal patients are generally offered tamoxifen for
five years, extended in higher-risk disease. Where risk warrants intensification, ovarian
function suppression may be added, and only in that combined setting does an aromatase
inhibitor become an option for a premenopausal patient. Postmenopausal patients are generally
offered an aromatase inhibitor, with tamoxifen reserved for those who cannot tolerate one.

**Comparative harms differ and matter to the conversation.** Tamoxifen carries
thromboembolic and endometrial risk; aromatase inhibitors carry arthralgia and accelerated
bone loss, so baseline bone density assessment is appropriate. Adherence over five to ten
years drives benefit more than the initial choice does, so tolerability is a legitimate
reason to switch classes.

Treatment decisions belong to the multidisciplinary team and the patient; decision-support
tools do not prescribe.

## Diagnostic guidance (2025-02) · Workup of a new discrete palpable breast mass

Scope: the first diagnostic encounter for an adult presenting with a new, discrete,
palpable lump. This document does not cover asymptomatic screening intervals, nipple
discharge without a mass, or post-treatment surveillance imaging.

1. Triple assessment means three concurrent legs — clinical examination, targeted
   imaging, and tissue sampling when indicated. A lump is not cleared until all
   applicable legs agree.
2. Imaging is chosen by age. Under approximately 30 years, begin with targeted
   ultrasound of the palpable site; add mammography only if ultrasound is suspicious
   or indeterminate. At 30 years and above, obtain diagnostic mammography (with
   tomosynthesis where available) together with targeted ultrasound.
3. During pregnancy or lactation, ultrasound is the first test at any age. Mammography
   remains permissible when needed; fetal dose from a shielded diagnostic study is
   negligible, and pregnancy is not a reason to defer diagnosis of a suspicious mass.
4. Place a radiopaque skin marker over the palpable abnormality so the radiologist
   images the same lesion the clinician felt. An unmarked study risks reporting a
   different, incidental finding.
5. Normal imaging does not exclude malignancy. If the mass is clinically suspicious —
   hard, fixed, irregular, with skin dimpling or nipple retraction — proceed to tissue
   sampling despite a negative ultrasound and mammogram.
6. Core needle biopsy is preferred over fine-needle aspiration because it preserves
   architecture and permits grading plus ER, PR, and HER2 testing. Reserve aspiration
   for draining a symptomatic simple cyst or sampling a suspicious axillary node.
7. A simple anechoic cyst with posterior enhancement needs no biopsy. Aspirate only for
   symptoms; if the aspirate is bloody or a residual mass persists after drainage,
   biopsy the residuum.
8. Complicated cysts, complex cystic-and-solid lesions, and any solid mass that is not
   a classically benign fibroadenoma warrant tissue diagnosis.
9. Deploy a marker clip at biopsy so the site can be relocated for surgery or after
   neoadjuvant therapy.
10. Every benign biopsy result must be reviewed for radiologic-pathologic concordance.

## Treatment guidance (2025-11-18) · Radiotherapy after breast-conserving surgery and after mastectomy

Scope: post-operative locoregional radiotherapy in non-metastatic disease. This note covers
indications and volumes. It does not cover systemic therapy selection.

**After breast-conserving surgery, radiotherapy is part of the operation, not an optional
extra.** Lumpectomy without irradiation carries a substantially higher rate of in-breast
recurrence, so whole-breast radiotherapy is the default for essentially every patient who
keeps her breast, including those with DCIS alone. Moderately hypofractionated schedules —
around fifteen to sixteen fractions over three weeks — are the standard of care for most
patients and are not an inferior compromise. A boost to the tumour bed is added for younger
patients, high-grade disease, or close margins, and can reasonably be omitted in an older
patient with low-grade, widely clear disease.

**Two situations are genuinely different from the default.** In a woman over about 65–70 with
a small, node-negative, hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative tumour excised with clear
margins, omitting whole-breast radiotherapy in favour of endocrine therapy alone is a
legitimate shared decision; local recurrence risk rises modestly while survival appears
unchanged, and the choice hinges on how the patient weighs those. Separately, partial-breast
irradiation is an option for carefully selected low-risk, node-negative tumours, and is not
appropriate for higher-risk or node-positive disease.

**After mastectomy, radiotherapy is indicated rather than routine.** Post-mastectomy
radiotherapy is recommended for four or more involved axillary nodes, for T3–T4 primaries,
for positive or persistently close margins, and for inflammatory breast cancer. With one to
three involved nodes it is discussed case by case, weighing age, grade, lymphovascular
invasion and receptor subtype. Where the axilla is treated, regional nodal irradiation
including the supraclavicular and internal mammary chains may be added; this is a separate
decision from chest wall treatment.

**Practical points.** Radiotherapy follows chemotherapy rather than running concurrently with
anthracyclines. Endocrine therapy may run alongside irradiation. Immediate reconstruction
does not remove an indication for radiotherapy, but it changes planning and reconstructive
sequencing, so the plastic surgery team should be involved before the mastectomy, not after.
Left-sided treatment should use cardiac-sparing technique such as deep inspiration breath
hold.

Treatment decisions belong to the multidisciplinary team and the patient; decision-support
tools do not prescribe.

## Treatment guidance (2025-09-30) · Neoadjuvant therapy: patient selection and assessment of response

Scope: systemic therapy delivered before surgery in non-metastatic disease. This note covers
who should be offered it and how response is judged. It does not cover choice of individual
cytotoxic agents.

**Two separate reasons to treat before operating.** The first is surgical: a large tumour in a
patient who wants breast conservation, or bulky nodal disease, may become operable or
conservable after downstaging. The second, and increasingly the more important, is
informational — the response of the tumour to chemotherapy is a strong prognostic signal, and
in triple-negative and HER2-positive disease that signal directly changes what is given after
surgery. A patient with residual disease can be offered escalated post-operative treatment
that would never have been identified had they gone straight to theatre.

**Who is a candidate.** Triple-negative and HER2-positive tumours of roughly 2 cm or larger,
or with clinically involved nodes, are the clearest candidates. Inflammatory breast cancer is
always treated systemically first. By contrast, strongly hormone-receptor-positive,
HER2-negative, low-grade tumours respond poorly to chemotherapy and rarely achieve a complete
response, so pre-operative chemotherapy is usually not the right tool for them; upfront
surgery is generally preferred unless downstaging is specifically needed.

**Before the first cycle.** Establish histological diagnosis with a core needle biopsy —
never fine-needle aspiration alone — with full receptor and HER2 testing. Place a radiopaque
marker clip in the tumour bed and in any biopsy-proven abnormal node, because a complete
response can erase the target and leave the surgeon nothing to excise. Baseline imaging should
be documented, and staging investigations completed for stage III or clinically suspicious
presentations.

**Assessing response.** Clinical examination and imaging are used mid-treatment mainly to
detect progression, which mandates re-evaluation of the plan; they do not reliably predict
the final pathological result. MRI correlates better than mammography but still over- and
under-estimates residual disease. The definitive endpoint is pathology at surgery: a
pathological complete response means no residual invasive carcinoma in the breast and no
nodal involvement, with residual DCIS still counted as a complete response by the usual
convention. Residual disease should be quantified in a structured way and reported to the
tumour board, since it determines post-operative escalation.

Treatment decisions belong to the multidisciplinary team and the patient; decision-support
tools do not prescribe.

Strongly hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative, low-grade tumors are generally not good candidates for pre-operative chemotherapy because they respond poorly and rarely achieve a complete response, making upfront surgery preferred unless downstaging is specifically needed [2025-09-30_guide_tx_neoadjuvant_selection_and_response.md]. ## Diagnostic guidance (2025-11) · Referral for genetic counselling and germline testing

Scope: which breast clinic patients should be referred for hereditary cancer counselling
and germline testing, and what the result changes. This concerns inherited variants in
blood or saliva. It does not cover somatic tumor sequencing, and it does not cover
multigene prognostic assays used to decide adjuvant chemotherapy.

1. Counselling precedes testing and follows it. The pre-test conversation covers what a
   result would change, implications for relatives, and reproductive and insurance
   consequences; the post-test conversation translates the report into management.
2. Refer any patient diagnosed with breast cancer at or under 45 years, irrespective of
   family history.
3. Refer a diagnosis at or under 50 when there is also a close relative with breast,
   ovarian, pancreatic, or high-risk prostate cancer, or when the patient has had a
   second primary breast cancer.
4. Refer triple-negative breast cancer diagnosed up to about age 60 regardless of family
   history; the yield of a BRCA1 variant in this group is high enough to justify testing
   on histology alone.
5. Refer every male breast cancer, at any age.
6. Refer bilateral disease, particularly when the first primary occurred before
   menopause.
7. Refer on family structure: two or more close relatives on the same side of the family
   with breast cancer, any relative with ovarian carcinoma, a constellation of breast
   with pancreatic or metastatic prostate cancer, or Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry with any
   affected relative.
8. When a pathogenic variant is already known in the family, test the patient for that
   specific variant first. A broad panel is unnecessary and complicates interpretation.
9. Invasive lobular carcinoma with a family history of diffuse gastric cancer should
   prompt consideration of CDH1.
10. Panels typically report high-penetrance genes including BRCA1, BRCA2, and PALB2;
    moderate-penetrance genes such as ATM and CHEK2; and syndromic genes including TP53,
    PTEN, and STK11. Penetrance differs enormously between these tiers and management
    must follow the tier, not merely the presence of a name on the report.
11. A pathogenic result changes real decisions: it reframes the discussion of
    contralateral risk-reducing mastectomy, prompts risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy
    for BRCA carriers, supports annual MRI surveillance, may open PARP inhibitor
    eligibility, and enables cascade testing of relatives.
12. A variant of uncertain significance is not actionable. Never plan surgery on a VUS.
13. A negative panel in a patient with a strong family history does not return her to
    average risk; her empiric risk still comes from the pedigree.

## Treatment guidance (2025-05-06) · Endocrine therapy: the tamoxifen versus aromatase-inhibitor decision

Scope: adjuvant endocrine therapy for hormone-receptor-positive invasive breast cancer. This
note covers only the choice between a selective estrogen receptor modulator and an aromatase
inhibitor, and the information required before that choice can be made.

**Menopausal status is a required input, not a refinement.** The two drug classes work by
different mechanisms, and the mechanism of one of them fails outright in the wrong patient.
Tamoxifen blocks the estrogen receptor and works regardless of where estrogen comes from.
Aromatase inhibitors — anastrozole, letrozole, exemestane — work by blocking peripheral
conversion of androgens to estrogen, which is the dominant source of estrogen only after the
ovaries have stopped producing it. Given alone to a patient with functioning ovaries, an
aromatase inhibitor does not adequately suppress estrogen and can provoke reflex ovarian
stimulation. Prescribing one without established menopausal status is therefore not a
cautious approximation; it is a potentially ineffective treatment.

**Consequently, an endocrine regimen cannot be selected from receptor status alone.** If a
request specifies "ER-positive, start endocrine therapy" without menopausal status, the
correct response is to decline to name an agent and to ask for the missing information. The
same applies when menopausal status is merely assumed from age: a 49-year-old may be
premenopausal or postmenopausal, and chemotherapy-induced amenorrhoea is not proof of
menopause because ovarian function can recover.

**Once status is established.** Premenopausal patients are generally offered tamoxifen for
five years, extended in higher-risk disease. Where risk warrants intensification, ovarian
function suppression may be added, and only in that combined setting does an aromatase
inhibitor become an option for a premenopausal patient. Postmenopausal patients are generally
offered an aromatase inhibitor, with tamoxifen reserved for those who cannot tolerate one.

**Comparative harms differ and matter to the conversation.** Tamoxifen carries
thromboembolic and endometrial risk; aromatase inhibitors carry arthralgia and accelerated
bone loss, so baseline bone density assessment is appropriate. Adherence over five to ten
years drives benefit more than the initial choice does, so tolerability is a legitimate
reason to switch classes.

Treatment decisions belong to the multidisciplinary team and the patient; decision-support
tools do not prescribe.


QUESTION: Anastrozole, letrozole, and exemestane are examples of which class of endocrine therapy?
Anastrozole, letrozole, and exemestane are examples of aromatase inhibitors. [2025-05-06_guide_tx_endocrine_tamoxifen_vs_ai.md]

## Diagnostic guidance (2025-06) · Screening intervals, risk stratification, and dense breasts

Scope: imaging of asymptomatic people for early detection, and how personal risk and
breast density modify the interval and the modality. Nothing here applies to a patient
with a symptom or to surveillance after a cancer diagnosis.

1. Screening presumes no symptoms. A palpable lump, skin change, or pathologic nipple
   discharge moves the patient into the diagnostic pathway immediately, whatever the
   date of her last normal screen. "She had a clear mammogram in March" is not a reason
   to wait.
2. For average-risk women, mammography is offered annually or biennially from the
   fifth decade, with many programs opening the discussion at 40. The choice of interval
   is a shared decision that should name the harms explicitly: recall for false
   positives, benign biopsy, and overdiagnosis of indolent disease.
3. Continue screening while the woman is in reasonable health and has a life expectancy
   of roughly ten years or more. Stop by comorbidity, not by birthday alone.
4. Digital breast tomosynthesis improves cancer detection and lowers recall compared
   with two-dimensional mammography, with the largest gain in non-fatty breasts.
5. Density is reported as a four-level category, from almost entirely fatty through
   heterogeneously dense to extremely dense. Density does two separate things: it masks
   cancers on mammography, and it is itself a modest independent risk factor.
6. For heterogeneously or extremely dense breasts in a woman who is otherwise average
   risk, supplemental whole-breast ultrasound or contrast-enhanced mammography finds
   additional cancers but raises false positives substantially. Offer it as a shared
   decision, not as an automatic add-on.
7. High risk is defined by a formal model that incorporates family structure and age at
   diagnosis in relatives, not by a vague sense that the history is bad. A lifetime risk
   at or above roughly 20 to 25% qualifies for intensified screening.
8. High-risk protocol is annual contrast-enhanced breast MRI added to annual
   mammography. For germline pathogenic variant carriers, MRI typically begins around
   age 25 to 30, with mammography deferred until about 30.
9. Women irradiated to the chest between ages 10 and 30, classically for Hodgkin
   lymphoma, begin annual MRI and mammography about eight years after radiotherapy and
   not before age 25.
10. Prior atypical ductal hyperplasia or lobular carcinoma in situ confers elevated
    risk. Consider supplemental MRI and discuss risk-reducing endocrine therapy.

For average-risk women, the choice of screening interval is a shared decision that should explicitly name the harms: recall for false positives, benign biopsy, and overdiagnosis of indolent disease. (2025-06-24_guide_dx_screening_intervals_risk_stratified.md)

## Diagnostic guidance (2025-05) · Reading BI-RADS assessment categories and the action each requires

Scope: how to interpret the final assessment category on a breast imaging report and
what management follows from it. This document concerns report interpretation only; it
does not tell you which imaging test to order first for a given symptom.

1. Category 0 — incomplete. The study cannot be finalized without additional views,
   ultrasound, or comparison with prior examinations. Category 0 is a workflow state,
   not a statement of risk. It is expected in screening recall and should be uncommon
   as the final result of a diagnostic study.
2. Category 1 — negative. Nothing to report. Return to the patient's routine screening
   interval.
3. Category 2 — benign. A specific benign entity is named: a coarsely calcified
   involuting fibroadenoma, a simple cyst, an intramammary lymph node, an oil cyst of
   fat necrosis, or a stable postsurgical scar. Management is identical to category 1 —
   routine screening — and no follow-up imaging is generated by the finding itself.
4. Category 3 — probably benign, carrying under roughly 2% likelihood of malignancy.
   The action is short-interval surveillance, conventionally at 6 months, then 12 and
   24 months, before the finding is downgraded to benign. Category 3 may be assigned
   only after a complete diagnostic workup, never off a screening study alone, and is
   inappropriate for a mass the patient can feel.
5. Category 4 — suspicious. Likelihood of malignancy spans roughly 2% to 95%, and
   tissue diagnosis is required. The subdivisions matter for counselling and for
   judging concordance afterwards: 4A low suspicion, 4B moderate suspicion, 4C high
   suspicion but short of classic malignant morphology.
6. Category 5 — highly suggestive of malignancy, at or above 95%. Biopsy is required,
   and surgical planning may proceed in parallel. A benign pathology result from a
   category 5 lesion is discordant by definition and mandates excision.
7. Category 6 — known biopsy-proven malignancy. It is applied to imaging performed
   after diagnosis, such as extent-of-disease mapping or response assessment during
   neoadjuvant therapy. It never means "biopsy again."
8. When a study shows several findings, the overall assessment takes the most abnormal
   category, and each breast is assessed separately.
9. Categories 4 and 5 require documented, tracked communication to the referring
   clinician; an unactioned suspicious report is a system failure, not a patient one.


QUESTION: What is the recommended management for a BI-RADS 3 lesion?

The recommended action for a BI-RADS 3 lesion is short-interval surveillance, conventionally at 6 months, then 12 and 24 months, before the finding is downgraded to benign. It is important to note that Category 3 may be assigned only after a complete diagnostic workup, never off a screening study alone, and is inappropriate for a mass the patient can feel.
